title: Taylor's Theorem with Remainder
short: f(x) = Pₙ(x) + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! for some c between a and x; a bound on f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ bounds the error.
trouble: Students use the nth derivative instead of the (n + 1)st, or plug in a guess for c instead of bounding the derivative over the whole interval.

blocks.html: In Calculus 2 you used Taylor's inequality to bound errors. Taylor's theorem says exactly what the error is, up to one unknown point, and it is the mean value theorem taken to higher order. (The case $n = 0$ is the MVT itself: $f(x) = f(a) + f'(c)(x - a)$.)

Taylor's theorem. If $f$ has $n + 1$ derivatives on an interval containing $a$ and $x$, then $$f(x) = P_n(x) + \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n + 1)!}(x - a)^{n+1}$$ for some $c$ between $a$ and $x$, where $P_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x - a)^{k}$. If $|f^{(n+1)}| \le M$ between $a$ and $x$, then $|f(x) - P_n(x)| \le \frac{M|x - a|^{n+1}}{(n + 1)!}$.

Fix $x \ne a$ and choose the number $K$ so that $g(t) = f(t) - P_n(t) - K(t - a)^{n+1}$ has $g(x) = 0$. By construction $g(a) = g'(a) = \cdots = g^{(n)}(a) = 0$. Rolle's theorem on $[a, x]$ gives $c_1$ with $g'(c_1) = 0$; Rolle again on $[a, c_1]$ (since $g'(a) = 0$) gives $c_2$ with $g''(c_2) = 0$; after $n + 1$ steps, $g^{(n+1)}(c) = 0$ for some $c$ between $a$ and $x$. But $g^{(n+1)}(t) = f^{(n+1)}(t) - (n + 1)!\,K$, because $P_n$ has degree $n$. So $K = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n + 1)!}$, which is the formula. $\blacksquare$

blocks.name: taylor
blocks.cap: Taylor polynomials of $e^{x}$ at $0$: add terms and watch the error at the probe point shrink like $\frac{3x^{n+1}}{(n + 1)!}$ predicts.

blocks.title: How many terms for $e$?
blocks.q: Approximating $e = e^{1}$ by $P_n(1) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{k!}$, using $e^{c} < 3$ for $0 \le c \le 1$, find the smallest $n$ with error bound below $0.001$.

blocks.title: A sine error
blocks.q: Bound the error of $\sin x \approx x - \frac{x^{3}}{6}$ at $x = \frac{1}{2}$.
steps: This is $P_3$ (the $x^{2}$ and $x^{4}$ terms are $0$, so it is also $P_4$). Using $P_4$: $|R_4| \le \frac{|x|^{5}}{5!}$ since every derivative of $\sin$ is at most $1$ in size.

blocks.title: Finding the point $c$
steps: $P_2 = 0$ (all derivatives up to order $2$ vanish at $0$), and $f'''(t) = 24t$.

blocks.html: The wrong derivative, or a guessed $c$. The remainder after $P_n$ uses the $(n + 1)$st derivative. And since $c$ is unknown, you cannot plug in $c = a$ or $c = x$; bound $|f^{(n+1)}|$ over the whole interval between $a$ and $x$ instead. For $e^{x}$ on $[0, 1]$ that bound is $e < 3$, not $e^{0} = 1$.
